items.title: Artificial photosynthesis uses waste CO₂ to grow protein-rich edible fungus in seven days
items.blurb: While many people think first of meat when they think about dietary protein, most protein ultimately depends on plants, since livestock feed on grass, hay and other plants. Meeting the demand for protein is taxing on the environment, requiring massive amounts of land and water while creating greenhouse gas emissions. And that demand is expected to require nearly 50% more agricultural production by 2050 than in 2012, according to the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization.

items.title: Draining peatlands leaves a long legacy of warming
items.blurb: Peatland ecosystems like bogs and swamps perform an important balancing act: Their vegetation takes up huge amounts of carbon dioxide, while their soil microbes produce methane. Although methane is a potent greenhouse gas, peatlands exhibit a net cooling effect on the planet because of the sheer scale of carbon dioxide they remove from the atmosphere, which has amounted to hundreds of gigatons globally over thousands of years.

items.title: Stabilizing atomically thin metals with sandwich structures: Machine learning expands the search
items.blurb: Atomically thin metals, metallenes, are promising materials for catalysis, electronics and energy conversion, but their synthesis has been challenging. Researchers from the University of Jyväskylä have now identified more than 300 stable metallene sandwich structures using machine learning and high-performance computing. The results provide researchers with a practical roadmap for the fabrication of new two-dimensional metals.

items.title: Smartphone app uses AI to identify illegal wildlife products

items.title: Certain fungi turn specialized plant cells into water-carrying cells using one protein
items.blurb: Can a pathogen that causes damage to a plant also make that plant more resilient to drought? An international research team led by the University of Göttingen has investigated this apparent paradox. The researchers discovered how certain fungi promote the formation of new water-conducting cells in plants. At the same time, infected plants showed increased tolerance to drought stress. The results were published in the journal Cell Host & Microbe.

items.title: Giant lambda-shaped stellar nursery found in the Milky Way's outskirts
items.blurb: Massive stars often form in dense regions, called "hubs," where filamentary structures made of star-forming materials meet. These star-forming complexes are "hub-filament" systems. Astronomers have discovered one such large network of molecular gas filaments in the outer regions of the Milky Way. It is called the λ-complex, and the structure is bigger than most known hub-filament systems. The research paper was published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society on Nov. 17.

items.title: Using lunar craters as free radiation shields for moon base nuclear reactors
items.blurb: Powering any future lunar base is a massive engineering challenge. The two-week lunar night can drain batteries charged by solar panels during the two-week day, if the batteries themselves can even withstand the freezing temperatures that go along with it. So, for decades at this point, engineers have planned to use a nuclear reactor to at least partially power any future human settlement on the moon.

items.title: Simulations reveal how a solar vortex and reconnecting magnetic fields can launch a rotating jet
items.blurb: Solar spicules are slender jets commonly found in the chromosphere. They lift relatively cool plasma from the lower solar atmosphere, carry energy upward, and in some cases rotate as they evolve. Small-scale vortices also occur frequently between convection-driven granules in the photosphere. Two questions remain incompletely answered: how these photospheric vortices help form spicules, and how much mass and energy the rising jets carry into the corona.

items.title: Without marine life, atmospheric CO₂ would shoot up by up to 65% by the end of the century

This is one of the main conclusions of the new policy brief developed within the framework of the European OceanICU project, which was presented at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Türkiye.

items.title: Structural agility of 2D crystals enables digital doping of graphene superlattices

items.title: Uterine pressure guides head-to-tail axis formation in mouse embryos
items.blurb: During animal development, the establishment of the three primary body axes—head-to-tail (anterior-posterior), dorsal-ventral and left-right—is essential for building a proper body structure. items.title: Errors in judging friendships predict who will connect or drift apart six months later

items.title: ceTDP: A Practical Tutorial on Valid and Quantitative Cluster-Extent Inference in Neuroimaging
items.blurb: We introduce ceTDP, a two-stage framework for cluster-extent inference in neuroimaging that extends conventional random field theory-based and permutation-based methods. In contrast to standard cluster inference, which yields binary significance, ceTDP additionally quantifies the proportion of truly active voxels within clusters using the true discovery proportion (TDP). The method is built on closed testing and provides strong family-wise error rate control while remaining consistent with standard cluster inference. The framework operates in two stages: estimation of a cluster-extent threshold, followed by computation of the TDP lower bound. Two complementary procedures are provided: a conservative, statistically guaranteed TDP lower bound (ceTDP-cons) and a heuristic approach for obtaining a potentially tighter estimate of the TDP lower bound (ceTDP-heur). Together, they enable both rigorous inference and improved sensitivity in cluster-level analysis.

items.title: A comprehensive Drosophila toolkit reveals context-dependent functional hierarchies across RasG12X variants in vivo
items.blurb: KRAS is a GTPase regulating key signalling processes involved in cell proliferation, differentiation, growth and survival. KRAS is the most prevalent oncogene in human cancers, often acquiring a point mutation at Glycine 12 (G12). Although several possible amino acid substitutions occur at this hotspot in humans, most animal cancer models often examine only a single or limited subset of G12X variants, restricting our understanding of their distinct biological effects. Here, we describe a novel transgenic toolkit in Drosophila melanogaster comparing the most frequently observed oncogenic G12X variants (G12A, G12C, G12D, G12R, G12S, G12V), and evaluate these across multiple developmental and tumour contexts in vivo. Interestingly, we demonstrate how the phenotypic strength of each G12X variant differs significantly depending on the biological context, highlighting the importance of considering these point mutations systematically. Overall, our comprehensive RasG12X toolkit provides a powerful and versatile platform to explore the dysregulation of KRAS in vivo, serving as a valuable resource enabling unprecedented opportunities to investigate variant- and context-specific mechanisms of oncogenic signalling with direct relevance to cancer biology and therapy.

items.title: An isogenic platform to model the impact of sex chromosome and donor genotype in hiPSC-derived vascular smooth muscle cells
items.blurb: Monosomy-X results in Turner Syndrome (TS), which beyond its cardinal height and reproductive phenotypes, spans incompletely penetrant cardiovascular phenotypes, including bicuspid valve, hypoplastic left-sided heart syndrome and aortic coarctation. These congenital heart defects (CHD) conspire with hypertension to dilate the ascending aorta, which can progress to rupture and drive early mortality in TS. Genetic contributors to incompletely penetrant phenotypes in TS remain only partially explored, thus complicating risk stratification. To begin addressing this challenge in donor-specific in-vitro models, we derived monosomy-X human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) alongside isogenic euploid control lines from donors mosaic for the second sex chromosome. In embryonic-origin specific vascular smooth muscle cells (vSMCs) derived from these hiPSCs, monosomy-X reveals donor-specific cellular and transcriptomic effects, with expression changes in one donor panel enriched in genes previously implicated in coronary artery disease and ascending aorta diameter. Polygenic risk scores (PGS) for cardiovascular traits mirror this transcriptomic enrichment, and suggest PGS analysis may help to prioritize hiPSC lines for in-vitro modeling of incompletely-penetrant traits related to TS-associated aortopathy.

items.title: Genetically Encoded Photodecaging of Asparagine Enables Protein Function Control and Time-Resolved N-Glycosylation
items.blurb: Asparagine contributes to protein function through its polar carboxamide side chain and serves as the acceptor residue for N-linked glycosylation, yet temporally controlling these roles directly through the side-chain carboxamide remains challenging. Here, we report the genetic encoding of N4-(2-nitrobenzyl)-L-asparagine (ONBN), a photocaged asparagine that regenerates the native side-chain carboxamide upon 365 nm irradiation. Engineered aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase/tRNA pairs enabled site-specific ONBN incorporation into proteins in Escherichia coli and mammalian cells. Photodecaging restored Renilla luciferase activity and activated TRAF6 polyubiquitination mediated by UBE2N in living cells. Beyond active-site residues, we further developed CAGE-proxN, using computationally guided proximal caging to optically activate firefly luciferase. Finally, ONBN incorporation at the acceptor position of an N-glycosylation sequon enabled light-triggered initiation and time-resolved monitoring of post-translational glycan installation on an endoplasmic reticulum-targeted reporter. Variation of the -2 flanking residue revealed sequence-dependent differences in apparent glycosylation kinetics. This work extends genetically encoded photocontrol to the asparagine carboxamide and provides a platform for investigating asparagine-dependent protein functions and the temporal regulation of N-glycosylation in living cells.

items.title: Self-generated action shapes theta phase alignment at encoding and later recollection
items.blurb: Across species, self-directed action is linked to theta rhythms and better memory, but such action combines choosing, moving, and controlling the outcome. Whether choosing and control over the outcome shape recollection, and the encoding dynamics that support it, remains unclear. Three preregistered experiments in human participants separated these components while holding movement constant. Participants encoded scene pairs by dragging either a freely chosen scene or one indicated by the program, with fluent or disrupted feedback. Recognition was tested after 24 hours (and immediately in Experiment 2), using Remember/Know judgments. Experiment 3 recorded scalp electroencephalography during encoding. Choosing improved recognition, more for recollection than familiarity. A smaller benefit extended to the unselected scene, although less consistently after latency adjustment. Disrupted feedback lowered rated agency but did not reduce memory at 24 hours. In Experiment 2, however, recollection declined less over 24 hours after self-generated than externally generated action, but only under fluent feedback. Choosing increased action-onset-locked theta and alpha phase alignment (inter-trial phase coherence), whereas disrupted feedback reduced alignment later. The selection effects survived matching for response-initiation-latency. Trial by trial, later posterior theta alignment (353-570 ms) predicted Remember over Know responses, whereas early frontal alpha alignment (127-245 ms) predicted Remember over Forgotten responses. These findings link self-generated action to the timing of encoding-related oscillations and to subsequent recollection. The association between later posterior theta alignment and Remember-Know discrimination is consistent with a role for theta phase coordination in associative binding.

items.title: FGF activates Wnt signaling during newt lens regeneration
items.blurb: Newts regenerate their eye lens following its complete removal. To accomplish this, pigmented epithelial cells located in the dorsal iris transdifferentiate to lens epithelial cells. FGF and Wnt signaling pathways have been implicated during this process, but their association remained unclear. Here, we used FGF signaling inhibitors to stall lens regeneration and studied the affected downstream mechanisms using immunofluorescence, western blotting, and RNAseq. We showed that entry to the cell cycle was slowed, ERK levels were lower, and several genes were differentially regulated with FGF inhibition. Among the impacted genes were Wnt signaling modulators revealing a potential connection between the pathways. FGF inhibition also stalled the gradual increase in beta-catenin abundance in the nucleus and junctions in iris pigmented epithelial cells during lens regeneration. To place Wnt downstream of the FGF signaling pathway, we pharmacologically activated Wnt and showed that it is sufficient to rescue the lens regeneration stalling phenotype observed with FGF inhibition. Overall, our data indicate that FGF activates the Wnt signaling pathway during newt lens regeneration.

items.title: Roe deer embryonic diapause is associated with reduced oxidative phosphorylation and altered lipid metabolism
items.blurb: Conceptus elongation is a shared feature of preimplantation development in roe deer and cattle. However, unlike cattle embryos, roe deer embryos undergo embryonic diapause prior to elongation, during which blastocyst growth remains markedly reduced for 4-5 months before development rapidly resumes. To investigate the molecular basis of these developmental differences, we assembled a novel roe deer reference genome and analyzed single-embryo transcriptomes from diapausing and elongated roe deer conceptuses, comparing their transcriptomes with those of cattle embryos from day 6 morulae to day 14 tubular conceptuses. Pseudotime and principal component analyses revealed parallel developmental trajectories across species and distinct gene-expression profiles during diapause. Roe deer diapause embryos exhibited reduced transcriptional signatures of oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial biogenesis and protein glycosylation pathways relative to cattle blastocysts, while maintaining expression of lineage-specification markers, consistent with continued differentiation despite a metabolically quiescent state. While roe deer retained the function of the corpus luteum during diapause and continued to secrete progesterone, they did not express interferon-{tau} upon elongation. Elongation of roe deer embryos triggered robust upregulation of cell-cycle regulators, ribosomal biogenesis and oxidative-phosphorylation genes, aligning with the high energetic demands of elongation. By contrasting a diapause and non-diapause species, we illuminated the genomic and metabolic frameworks that underlie this unique reproductive adaptation of diapause and elongation.

items.title: PMRIPrep: automated preprocessing and quantification of DSC and DCE MRI
items.blurb: While dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC) MRI measures hemodynamics and dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI characterizes vascular permeability, quantitative values from both modalities remain processing-dependent. We present PMRIPrep, a Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) App for automated DSC and DCE preprocessing and quantification. PMRIPrep adapts to available acquisitions and metadata, integrates both modalities within a session, and supports four DSC deconvolution methods and four DCE pharmacokinetic models. In DSC simulations with 4% cerebral blood volume and signal-to-noise ratio 50, pooled median absolute cerebral blood flow error was 13-19% across methods. Median Ktrans bias remained [≤]2% across four model-matched DCE configurations over 0-10% noise. End-to-end OSIPI analyses yielded DCE accuracy and clinical test-retest repeatability scores of 0.85 and 0.85, respectively. Outputs follow BIDS-Derivatives conventions and include machine-readable provenance and visual quality-control reports. PMRIPrep is freely available as a containerized application.

items.title: Continuous ex utero development of mouse zygotes to early organogenesis
items.blurb: In mammals, embryogenesis normally unfolds within the uterus, limiting direct access to the developmental processes that transform a zygote into an embryo with forming organs. Although mouse embryos can be cultured ex utero from early post-implantation stages to mid-gestation, continuous culture from the zygote into organogenesis has not been achieved. Through comparative single-cell transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses, here we discover aberrant BMP signaling and suboptimal metabolic support as barriers to continuous ex utero development. BMP inhibition, together with stage-specific optimization of the culture environment, enables mouse zygotes to progress through peri-implantation development, gastrulation, and into early organogenesis ex utero. Cultured embryos form major embryonic and extraembryonic lineages, establish body axes, and generate multiple organ primordia, while retaining developmental delays and molecular differences from in vivo embryos. By connecting developmental stages that have previously been cultured separately, this study provides an accessible platform for dissecting how early mammalian development progresses into organ formation and a reference for evaluating stem-cell-based embryo models.

items.title: The emergence and neural organisation of facial-expression information during ultra-brief vision
items.blurb: A glimpse lasting only a few milliseconds can convey meaningful information about a face, but how the brain transforms such minimal input into stable representations of facial expression and conscious experience remains unclear. Across two experiments using ultra-brief face presentations, we combined hierarchical psychophysical modelling, multivariate EEG decoding, and information-theoretic measures to characterise this transformation. Extending previously reported findings, hierarchical modelling quantified distinct exposure-dependent trajectories for intact-face localisation and expression identification, providing a behavioural calibration of weak, intermediate, and stronger perceptual evidence. The critical neural transition occurred between 4.4 and 6.2 ms. At 4.4 ms, expression sensitivity was behaviourally detectable, but neural expression patterns did not reliably generalise to faces excluded from classifier training. At 6.2 ms, previously observed emotion-related ERP differences were accompanied by expression representations that generalised across faces and locally detectable emotion information during the early posterior negativity (EPN) interval. Subjective clarity tracked location-related neural evidence more consistently than expression-specific evidence, indicating that awareness did not simply mirror the emerging expression representation. The degree to which early centroparietal activity statistically predicted later occipital activity differed between emotional and neutral faces as exposure increased, indicating that the relationship between successive neural responses was reorganised. Thus, a few additional milliseconds of visual input did not merely strengthen facial-expression processing; they transformed weak evidence that did not reliably generalise across faces into more stable, generalisable, behaviourally relevant, and distributed neural information.

items.title: Archetypal analysis provides interpretable mixture representations of microbiome community structure
items.blurb: Microbiome studies routinely reduce high-dimensional community profiles to a small number of coordinates for visualization and comparison. Ordination methods are powerful for detecting compositional differences, but their axes are often difficult to translate into explicit microbial community configurations; conversely, hard clustering can impose discrete states on variation that is frequently continuous. Here we evaluate Archetypal Analysis (AA) as an intermediate representation in which each microbiome is expressed as a convex combination of a small number of data-supported extreme community profiles. Across three applications, AA recovered biologically recognizable structure while preserving graded variation among samples. In a multi-biospecimen human microbiome dataset, different sample-source categories occupied characteristic regions of archetype space, while stool samples were represented by heterogeneous mixtures of archetypal profiles. In an early-life gut microbiome dataset, archetype usage changed systematically with age, describing microbial succession as changing contributions from community endpoints. In domestic dogs spanning forager, agrarian, pastoralist, urban, and industrialized lifestyles, groups showed characteristic but non-discrete combinations of archetypes, supporting generality across host species and ecological contexts. Across the displayed K-sensitivity analyses, the principal sample-source and early-life organization remained recognizable as model resolution changed, while repeated initialization and resampling analyses recovered similar archetypal structure. Held-out samples projected onto fixed training-derived archetypes retained metadata-associated organization within each dataset. Bray-Curtis principal coordinates analysis recovered the same broad biological structure, indicating that the value of AA is interpretive rather than simply greater separation, while taxa prioritized by AA retained substantial predictive information relative to equally sized random taxon sets. Together, these results support AA as a complementary microbiome representation that connects low-dimensional sample coordinates directly to interpretable taxonomic profiles and provides a natural framework for describing ecological states, gradients, and transitions without hard cluster assignments.

items.title: Actionable, Motivating, and Not Beyond Question: Student Insights On AI-Enabled Feedback and Instructor AI Use
items.blurb: Scientific writing helps students develop and communicate their understanding through practices such as constructing explanations and arguing from evidence, but its complexity often requires individualized feedback and guidance. This makes scientific writing a worthwhile context in which to study the effects of feedback augmentation with generative AI (genAI). Although emerging work demonstrates that genAI can support feedback generation, considerably less is known about how students experience and respond to AI-enabled feedback. At the same time, feedback research has identified characteristics students view as supportive, yet it remains unclear whether these insights apply to AI-enabled feedback. Accordingly, this qualitative study examines biology students' experiences and perceptions of feedback developed by their instructor with assistance from a custom genAI tool in an authentic learning context. Analysis of student team interviews developed three themes: students recognized characteristics of effective feedback, positive emotions encouraged intention to revise, and students accepted but critically evaluated instructor AI use. Together, the themes suggest that AI-enabled feedback supported revision through both its content and its influence on students' academic emotions, which contributed to more favorable views of instructor genAI use. However, students' evaluations also depended on whether AI use aligned with their expectations and on the credibility of both the instructor and the genAI tool, for which instructor oversight was an important consideration. Collectively, these findings highlight the importance of a learner-centered approach to genAI implementation that accounts for students' needs and expectations and promotes engagement with feedback. Together, these findings suggest that students' positive perceptions of AI-enabled feedback were rooted less in the use of AI itself and more in the extent to which the feedback supported revision and improvement.

items.title: CSF Boundary Disruption and Tumor-Dependent Patterns of Medulloblastoma Metastasis
items.blurb: Background: Leptomeningeal metastasis is the major cause of mortality in medulloblastoma, yet the mechanisms that facilitate dissemination are poorly resolved. Here, we leveraged preclinical models to define metastatic topology, the anatomical distribution and organization of disseminated disease across craniospinal compartments and ask how topology is influenced by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) access, primary tumor anatomy, and tumor biology. Methods: Orthotopic D425 xenograft models were used to manipulate primary tumor geometry, defined by anatomical position of primary tumors within the cerebellum relative to CSF facing boundaries. Longitudinal bioluminescence, survival, primary growth architecture at the tumor host interface, CSF boundary breach, and craniospinal metastatic distribution were quantified. Additional medulloblastoma models MED411, MED2112, and CHLA-01-MED were implanted at a common midline cerebellar location to assess tumor-intrinsic contributions to metastatic topology. Results: While primary tumor geometry altered disease progression and survival, it did not significantly alter metastasis distribution. Strikingly, growth architecture and primary tumor burden correlated with dissemination. Despite their large size, circumscribed tumors frequently remained localized, whereas smaller, disruptive primary growth architecture was strongly associated with boundary breach, intracranial, and spinal dissemination. Conversely, when anatomical origin was held constant, distinct medulloblastoma models generated significantly different metastatic topologies. Conclusions: Disruption of CSF-facing anatomical boundaries is associated with distant dissemination, whereas the distribution of established metastatic disease differs substantially among medulloblastoma models despite standardized implantation conditions. These findings distinguish anatomical factors associated with dissemination from tumor-dependent patterns of metastatic colonization and establish an experimental framework for investigating the mechanisms underlying metastatic topology.

items.title: Single-cell Morphological Mechanisms-of-Action Profiling using Nanowell Imaging Plates
items.blurb: Mechanism-of-action (MoA) analysis is used in drug discovery to prioritize compounds that act through desired pathways while eliminating compounds associated with nonspecific or undesirable activity. Image cytometry provides a promising route for MoA inference by capturing high-dimensional cellular phenotypes at single-cell resolution, but conventional workflows remain limited by unreliable cell segmentation and dependence on human-engineered feature extraction. Here, we present a deep learning-based image cytometry workflow that confines single cells in nanowells to obtain uniformly framed, regularized single-cell images, enabling MoA inference directly from raw images without segmentation or human-engineered features. Using a nanowell-in-microwell platform, we treated cells with 21 chemotherapeutic compounds spanning 11 MoA classes across multiple doses and time points, generating more than 500,000 single-cell images for model training and validation. A ResNet-18 convolutional neural network trained on images annotated by known compound mechanism achieved 85% accuracy in MoA classification. When a second model was trained on compound identity rather than MoA, misclassification patterns frequently linked compounds with shared mechanisms, indicating that the model learned mechanism-level relationships directly from single-cell morphology, without those relationships being specified in advance. Together, these results establish regularized single-cell imaging in nanowells as a scalable and interpretable approach to image-based MoA classification that overcomes key limitations of segmentation-dependent feature analysis.

items.title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Vascular Wall Cells during Ductus Arteriosus Development and Closure
items.blurb: Background: The transition from fetal to postnatal circulation requires closure of the ductus arteriosus (DA), involving smooth muscle cell contraction followed by anatomical remodeling. However, the spatial organization and developmental transcriptional dynamics of vascular wall cells during this transition remain poorly understood. Methods: We analyzed vascular morphology and spatial transcript profiles of the mouse DA and aorta at five stages from embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5) to postnatal day 2.5 (P2.5), enabling paired comparisons within tissue sections. Selected findings were compared with an independent mouse single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset. Histological and spatial transcript analyses were also performed on human DA tissue and the adjacent pulmonary artery. Results: The DA exhibited transiently higher cell-cycle-associated transcription across multiple vascular wall populations at E16.5, preceding medial thickening at E18.5 and postnatal luminal closure. Prenatally, DA mural cells exhibited greater contractile-associated gene expression than aortic mural cells. This difference diminished after birth, accompanied by a marked shift toward synthetic-like transcriptional programs associated with extracellular matrix remodeling and proteolysis. Ductal endothelial cells exhibited postnatal divergence from aortic endothelial cells in matrix- and adhesion-associated gene expression. Adventitial fibroblasts displayed distinct extracellular matrix- and insulin-like growth factor-associated expression profiles. In a human postnatal DA specimen, synthetic-like mural cells were enriched in regions of disrupted elastic lamellae and prominent collagen staining and shared selected remodeling-associated markers with postnatal mouse DA mural cells. Conclusions: DA development and closure involve temporally organized transcriptional changes across vascular wall populations, characterized by prenatal cell-cycle-associated activity and rapid postnatal reorganization of mural transcriptional programs. These findings provide a spatial framework for understanding vascular cell plasticity and multicellular remodeling during DA closure.

items.title: DDB2 localizes to the nucleolus to mediate oxaliplatin resistance in colorectal cancer
items.blurb: Despite the widespread use of platinum drugs in cancer therapy, defining their mechanisms of action and predicting clinical outcomes remain challenging. Unlike cisplatin, which kills cells mainly through the DNA damage response, oxaliplatin toxicity is driven largely by nucleolar stress, yet how cells cope with this stress remains poorly understood. A nucleotide excision repair protein, damage-specific DNA binding protein 2 (DDB2), protects cells from oxaliplatin but not cisplatin, suggesting that it may preferentially engage oxaliplatin adducts. Using single-molecule analysis of DNA-binding proteins from nuclear extracts, we show that DDB2 binds both oxaliplatin and cisplatin intrastrand adducts. Oxaliplatin, but not cisplatin, drives progressive accumulation of DDB2 in nucleoli, pointing to a role at sites of oxaliplatin-induced nucleolar stress. The repair-deficient xeroderma pigmentosum group E K244E variant localizes to nucleoli but fails to rescue oxaliplatin sensitivity of DDB2-knockout cells, indicating that repair activity, not nucleolar localization alone, is required for protection. In colorectal cancer (CRC), elevated DDB2 levels correlate with higher oxaliplatin IC50, are higher in tumors than adjacent normal tissue by immunohistochemistry, and DDB2 transcript associates with non-response and shorter progression-free survival in FOLFOX-treated patients. Pharmacological inactivation or degradation of DDB2 synergizes with oxaliplatin, offering a biomarker-driven strategy to overcome chemoresistance.

items.title: A conserved ubiquitin signalling module controls membrane raft integrity at the neuronal synapse
items.blurb: Activity-dependent ubiquitination of synaptic proteins is one of the key contributors of synaptic plasticity, along with localized protein synthesis and ubiquitin-dependent protein turnover. Substantial changes in the protein composition occur in the postsynaptic density upon chronic activation or inhibition of primary neurons. Precisely how a large-scale regulation of ensembles of synaptic proteins occurs through the ubiquitin proteasome system remains unknown. MAGE-D1 is a highly conserved protein enriched in brain and its deletion in mice leads to a range of behavioral phenotypes including defects in learning, memory and a complete resistance to cocaine addiction. Here, we found that MAGE-D1 acts as a scaffold bridging the ubiquitin ligase Praja-1 and the deubiquitinase Usp7. This MAGE-D1 signalling module directly interacts with and regulates the levels of Brain acid-soluble protein-1 (BASP1) which is a key component and stabilizer of neuronal membrane rafts. Disruption of MAGE-D1 complex function or chemical inhibition of Usp7 in mice results in resistance to cocaine-induced locomotor sensitization accompanied by specific degradation of oligomeric BASP1 and other key synaptic proteins in the postsynaptic density of mice thalamus. As a result, loss of MAGE-D1 in differentiated neurons leads to a dramatic disorganization of neuronal membrane rafts and anomalies in the synaptic membrane protein landscape. Finally, we mapped the structural architecture of the human MAGE-D1/Praja-1/Usp7 complex revealing the basis for the scaffolding nature of MAGE-D1. In summary, we discovered a conserved synaptic ubiquitin signalling network mediated by a protein complex that localizes to the synapse and regulates structures of membrane rafts and actin cytoskeleton.

items.title: Nerve and vascular abnormalities precede loss of corneal transparency in Pax6-haploinsufficient mice
items.blurb: Aniridia-associated keratopathy (AAK), caused by PAX6 haploinsufficiency, progresses from a clinically clear cornea to opacity, neovascularization, and abnormal innervation, but when disease-associated changes first emerge remains unclear. We combined corneal nerve imaging, CD31 immunolabeling, transmission electron microscopy, and RNA sequencing of whole cornea from Pax6Sey-Neu/+mice at postnatal day 3-4, day 15, and adulthood. Corneal transcripts were analyzed using curated axon-guidance, myelination, and vascular/lymphatic gene panels. Mutant corneas showed reduced nerve density and persistent stromal fascicles beginning during the first postnatal week. Peripheral vascular structures were present in both genotypes at birth; these resolved during normal maturation but persisted and extended centrally in mutant corneas by two weeks, before loss of transparency. Transcriptomic analysis identified widespread differences between genotypes while both corneas remained transparent, with the strongest and most coherent changes involving vascular and lymphatic genes. Wild-type corneas silenced an endothelial and lymphatic expression program between postnatal day 15 and adulthood, whereas mutant corneas retained expression of this program. Individual axon-guidance genes differed between genotypes, but axon-guidance did not show program-level expansion in transparent corneas. Compact stromal myelin was restricted to opaque regions. These findings identify early vascular and neural abnormalities that precede corneal opacity and establish that a transparent Pax6-haploinsufficient cornea is already pathologically altered.

items.title: mRNA-1273.262 and mRNA-1283.262 Vaccines Expressing XFG Antigens Neutralize Relevant Circulating Variants
items.blurb: SARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate and causes substantial disease burden as an endemic respiratory pathogen. Vaccination is a key public health measure to ameliorate the effects of COVID-19 disease but requires annual update to match strains that are circulating. Monitoring of circulating virus and characterization of matched candidate vaccines helps to inform which antigens will provide the greatest benefit to public well-being. The 2026-2027 season will leverage XFG as the variant of interest for vaccine production and in vitro and in vivo data was generated preclinically to support this selection. XFG variant vaccines express well in mRNA format as both full-length spike and linked subdomain antigen formats. Animals immunized with these vaccines elicit robust neutralizing responses to relevant JN.1-family virus variants in both primary series and booster models. In future seasons, robust epidemiologically monitoring including viral genome sequencing will improve early detection of relevant variants and subsequent preparation of vaccine antigens.

items.title: Prioritization over certainty: Action planning in visual working memory iscoupled with selective attention, rather than action predictability
items.blurb: When visual information is no longer perceptually available, working memory (WM) allows us to act on sensory representations. But does this guidance require attentional prioritization? We addressed this question by asking participants to remember two oriented bars that were later tested with one predictable and one random probe. This design allowed us to track when a remembered orientation became linked to a specific response hand and whether that link depended on which item was currently prioritized in WM. Response preparation followed prioritization: even when the later response was predictable, no motor preparation emerged while the corresponding item remained latent. Our exploratory analyses showed that prospective action information reduced the need to reprioritize latent items, and that learned stimulus-response mappings generalized across task contexts, suggesting that task-relevant features of visual WM can be partly offloaded onto motor codes. These findings show that active response preparation is coupled with selective attention, while motor representations can also support maintenance in a visual WM task.

items.title: GESTATIONAL PROTEIN RESTRICTION PROGRAMS SEXUALLY DIVERGENT BEHAVIORAL AGING IN MICE: EARLY AFFECTIVE VULNERABILITY IN MALES AND LATE-LIFE MNEMONIC PRESERVATION AT A HEDONIC COST IN FEMALES
items.blurb: Maternal protein restriction is a well-established model of developmental programming, yet its consequences for behavior and cognition across the second half of life, and how these differ between sexes, remain poorly characterized. We fed C57BL/6J dams a normal-protein (NP, 17%) or low-protein (LP, 6%) diet throughout gestation and followed male and female offspring with an integrated battery assessing reward sensitivity, locomotion, anxiety-like behavior, social behavior, recognition memory, spatial learning and cognitive flexibility at 12 (middle age) and 18 months (old age). Maternal care was quantified from postnatal days 2 to 9. LP offspring of both sexes were born lighter and caught up by postnatal day 7. LP dams spent more time self-grooming, with longer self-grooming bouts, and took longer to retrieve their pups, whereas licking/grooming, its fragmentation and nursing were unchanged. Middle-aged LP males showed anhedonia-like behavior, anxiety-like behavior in the elevated plus-maze, reduced exploration and impaired short-term object recognition; in old age, affective indices normalized, but males became hyperactive and used less efficient search strategies in the Barnes maze. Middle-aged LP females showed hyperactivity, stereotypy and thigmotaxis; at 18 months they developed anhedonia-like behavior yet retained long-term object, social and spatial memory that had declined in aged NP females. A qualitative comparison with a prenatal-stress cohort tested in the same laboratory with the same battery revealed an overlapping, sex- and age-specific signature, particularly for the timing of anhedonia and for late-life memory outcomes. Gestational protein restriction, therefore, programs domain-specific and sexually divergent behavioral aging trajectories rather than uniform cognitive decline. These findings support sex-stratified, life-course designs in fetal programming research.

items.title: A tuned topographic map hierarchy formats visual working memory load
items.blurb: Visual working memory tasks rely on neural systems that scale activity with task load. Traditional models assume higher demands are met by monotonically increasing activity within a single process, implying high informational redundancy across responses. However, theories of cognitive control suggest processing strategies change with task demands, flexibly linking sensory inputs to behavior. Using 7T fMRI and neural encoding models, we hypothesized and confirmed that association cortices format task load-dependent responses using sensory-like neural tuning. We identified populations selectively tuned to specific loads, forming 11 topographic maps per hemisphere hierarchically organized from posterior sensory to anterior executive regions across a fronto-parieto-occipital network. Tuning persisted across performance and trial-order controls, was absent without memory task demands, and predicted behavioral accuracy after load changes. These findings demonstrate that human association cortices distribute task demands using continuously varying processing pathways, adapting sensory-like tuning to decorrelate responses and reduce information redundency during cognitive control.

items.title: Constraint-Based Pan-Cancer Metabolic Modeling Identifies Medium-Robust Biomarkers and Broad-Spectrum Anticancer Targets
items.blurb: Background: Cancer metabolic reprogramming varies across tumour types and nutrient environments, complicating the identification of robust metabolic biomarkers and therapeutic targets. We developed a constraint based pancancer framework to identify medium robust metabolic alterations and broadly effective candidate enzyme targets. Methods: Transcriptomic profiles from 33 TCGA cancer types were integrated with Recon3D to reconstruct cancer and healthy tissue specific genome scale metabolic models. Parsimonious multiobjective metabolite flow variability analysis was performed under five nutrient conditions to classify differential rates of metabolite synthesis, uptake, and secretion. An extended Anticancer Target Discovery framework incorporating fuzzy multiobjective optimization was employed to evaluate candidate enzyme perturbations based on cancer cell inhibition, ATP suppression, preservation of healthy tissue metabolism, and robustness across nutrient conditions. Findings: The models predicted recurrent increases in cardiolipin-related lipid synthesis and aromatic amino acid metabolism, enhanced uptake of essential amino acids and choline, and elevated lactate secretion across multiple cancer medium combinations. CRLS1 emerged as the most broadly effective predicted enzyme target, satisfying the treatment criteria across all 165 cancer medium combinations, whereas PGS1 and PTPMT1 exhibited broad but incomplete coverage. These findings highlight mitochondrial phospholipid metabolism as a potential shared vulnerability across cancer types and provide testable candidates for metabolomic and experimental validation.

items.title: Interpreting citizen science data for larval surveillance: lessons from storm drain reports in Mosquito Alert
items.blurb: Mosquito-borne diseases are an increasing public health concern, and urban drainage infrastructure such as storm drains and catch basins can provide breeding habitat for Aedes vectors, including Aedes albopictus. Detecting these sites over large areas is costly with traditional surveillance alone, and citizen science offers a complementary, lower-cost source of geolocated observations. Mosquito Alert is a citizen science platform, active since 2014, through which participants report adult mosquitoes, bites, and potential breeding sites. In this work, we present a descriptive analysis of the 17,880 storm drain breeding sites reported through the platform from June 2014 to August 2026, obtained from the project's public map. We counted the reported sites by country and geographic coordinate, examined when reports are submitted and which fields are recorded, estimated how often water and larvae are reported, and mapped the records globally. We also developed an interactive map to help inspect regions where many records overlap. Spain accounts for 90% of the records, 82% of all reports were submitted between April and June, and half of them fall on only 50 days. Group events, defined as five or more users reporting in the same municipality on the same day, account for 63% of the records. Water was reported in 43% of the storm drains: 33% in group events and 61% in the remaining reports. Larvae information exists for only 1,739 records; almost all are drains with water, and 28.5% of those had larvae, with higher shares in the warmer months and where participants noticed adult mosquitoes nearby. Our aim is not to model mosquito populations but to describe the structure of the data and highlight patterns worth further investigation. Because citizen science reporting effort varies across space, time, and socioeconomic groups, we discuss how sampling bias and other limitations of volunteer-based data affect the interpretation of these patterns and what they imply for the use of such data in larval surveillance.

items.title: Autumn warming decouples the molecular control of photosynthesis and cold acclimation from growth cessation in white spruce
items.blurb: {middle dot} In evergreen conifers, late-season photosynthetic downregulation is typically coordinated with growth cessation and the induction of cold acclimation, a key component of winter adaptation. However, the transcriptional basis of this coordination and its sensitivity to warming and drought remain poorly understood. {middle dot} To investigate the molecular basis of these responses, we examined how summer drought, autumn warming and their combination affect the expression of photosynthetic and cold-acclimation genes in white spruce, and whether responses differ among families from different latitudes. {middle dot} Autumn warming sustained photosynthetic gene expression into early winter while suppressing cold-acclimation genes, demonstrating that photosynthetic and cold-acclimation networks become decoupled from growth cessation, which remained largely unchanged. Although cold acclimation models derived from herbaceous species predict regulation through CBF pathways, canonical CBF/DREB regulators showed little transcriptional response. Instead, warming-induced suppression of cold acclimation was mediated by MYB- and AP2/ERF-centered regulatory networks, indicating a distinct conifer mechanism. Northern and southern families also differed in their transcriptional responses to warming despite exhibiting similar growth-cessation phenology. {middle dot} Together, these findings identify regulatory networks through which warmer autumns disrupt seasonal coordination in boreal conifers, potentially increasing susceptibility to freezing injury, limiting spring recovery, and ultimately affecting forest carbon sequestration.

items.title: Targeting ATR-CHK1-WEE1 signaling enhances IMPDH inhibitor efficacy in mTORC1-driven tumor cells
items.blurb: Uncontrolled activation of the master metabolic regulator Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin Complex 1 (mTORC1) in tumors confers strong dependence on the guanylate nucleotide synthesis enzyme inosine-5'-monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH) for tumor cell growth and viability. Clinically approved IMPDH inhibitors reduce the guanylate nucleotide pool available for DNA synthesis in mTORC1-driven tumor cells, resulting in prolonged DNA replication stress and accumulation of DNA damage that culminates in apoptosis. These early molecular events are accompanied by activation of adaptive DNA replication stress response (RSR) and DNA damage response (DDR) pathways. We hypothesized that targeting these adaptive responses could enhance IMPDH inhibitor efficacy. We find that combining IMPDH inhibition with inhibition of the ATR-CHK1-WEE1 signaling axis increases the efficacy and durability of response in cell models, and in a syngeneic xenograft tumor model of the mTORC1-driven genetic tumor syndrome Tuberous Sclerosis Complex. Mechanistically, abrogating ATR-CHK1-WEE1 signaling during prolonged IMPDH inhibition causes aberrant cell cycle progression, increased DNA double-strand breaks, and formation of micronuclei. Together these findings uncover adaptive mechanisms that restrict IMPDH inhibitor efficacy, informing a combination strategy to improve treatment efficacy, while maintaining selectivity for targeting tumor cells that are driven by uncontrolled mTORC1 activation.

items.title: Fishing for new immunotherapy compounds to boost innate tumor rejection
items.blurb: Despite significant advances in cancer immunotherapy, tackling immunosuppression remains critical to achieve more effective responses. While developing the zebrafish xenograft model, we found that some human tumors engraft very efficiently ("progressors"), while others are cleared by the host ("regressors"). We showed that this was dependent on innate immunity, which recognizes and eliminates some cancer cells, while others are able to evade and suppress it. This opened an opportunity to perform an in vivo phenotypic drug screen to find compounds that induce clearance by boosting innate-tumor rejection. Zebrafish xenografts of human colorectal (CRC) and breast cancer (BC) that show a high engraftment/low clearance phenotype were used to screen over 500 FDA-approved small-molecule compounds, with tumor clearance serving as the phenotypic readout. The screen identified 23 hit compounds, of which six were effective across both cancer models. Mechanism-of-action enrichment analysis revealed a significant overrepresentation of autonomic nervous system-targeting drugs among the hits, particularly cholinergic ones. Immune profiling in myeloid reporter lines showed that the lead hit, Tiotropium bromide, a muscarinic receptor antagonist, reprograms tumor-associated macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory, anti-tumoral state. Tiotropium significantly increased macrophage phagocytosis, and macrophage depletion completely abolished its pro-clearance activity, establishing these myeloid cells as essential effectors. In a syngeneic CT26 colorectal mouse model, Tiotropium synergized with anti-PD-1 to control tumor growth and improve survival, outperforming all monotherapy arms. This effect was immune-dependent, as it was lost in immunodeficient NSG mice. Together, these findings demonstrate that in vivo phenotypic screening of FDA-approved compounds in zebrafish xenografts is a productive strategy for innate immune drug discovery in cancer. The identification of Tiotropium as a myeloid-reprogramming innate immune primer, together with the unbiased recovery of the neuro-immune axis as a druggable target, opens new avenues for overcoming immunotherapy resistance.

items.title: mRNAspect: Real-Time Quality Control of Therapeutic mRNA with N1-Methylpseudouridine Bias Correction Using Nanopore Direct RNA Sequencing
items.blurb: Quality attributes of therapeutic mRNA include sequence identity, transcript completeness, and poly(A) tail length. While these attributes require monitoring from development through manufacturing, each needs a separate assay. Nanopore direct RNA sequencing enables rapid quality control because it measures all three on the same molecules within a single run, and the resulting data are available during sequencing. However, N1-methylpseudouridine (m1{Psi}), which often replaces uridine in therapeutic mRNAs, alters the nanopore signal, biasing basecalling and poly(A) estimation. We present mRNAspect, a pipeline combining real-time analysis and m1{Psi} bias correction. mRNAspect includes a fine-tuned basecaller and a poly(A) correction based on the reference sequence. mRNAspect is a packaged macOS app that ingests POD5 or BAM files by watching the MinKNOW output directory as sequencing proceeds. Its graphical user interface shows the latest snapshot of the results, and it writes HTML reports as each input file is processed and a PDF report when the run is finished. When measured on Linux with a single NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti, each 3-min batch of sequencing (about 5,700 reads) was processed in 38 s. The basecaller was fine-tuned on in vitro transcribed (IVT) constructs and cDNA-IVT libraries. Across 10 m1{Psi} constructs held out from training, the fine-tuned basecaller reduced the error rate from 20.1% to 7.2%, compared with 3.0% for unmodified RNA. A poly(A) correction was fitted to constructs with both modified and unmodified pairs. The correction accounts for the fraction of uridine in the reference sequence and the number of uridines within the 12-nt sequence adjacent to the tail. Across eight constructs, the correction reduced the poly(A) tail length difference between modified and unmodified pairs from up to 9.0 nt to within 1.8 nt.

items.title: TEMPLE-MEASURED POSTPRANDIAL CARDIOVASCULAR RESPONSES UNDER FREE-LIVING CONDITIONS
items.blurb: Eating perturbs cardiovascular homeostasis: splanchnic vasodilation after a meal is offset by autonomic adjustments that raise heart rate, and both the magnitude and duration of this response can depend on meal size and composition. Measuring these responses in daily life requires knowing when each meal begins and ends, which self-report captures poorly. The temple region allows both to be measured with a single device: chewing-related motion over the temporalis can mark meal onset and offset, and photoplethysmography (PPG) at the superficial temporal artery (STA) records the cardiovascular response. The STA also supplies a vascular bed whose postprandial behavior has not been well characterized. Using a temple-worn wearable under free-living conditions, we asked (1) whether established postprandial heart rate (HR) responses can be observed from automatically detected meals, and (2) how PPG pulse morphology at the STA changes after a meal. One meal from each of 100 participants in free-living conditions was analyzed, comparing a 15-min pre-meal baseline with the 120 min after eating, with nutrient content estimated from meal photographs. HR rose approximately 2.6 bpm on average in the first 15 min after eating and approached baseline within two hours. The postprandial rise in HR increased with caloric content. HR remained elevated two hours after the most sodium-dense meals, whereas higher fiber density was associated with a larger rise only during the first 15 minutes. The heart-rate increase per 100 kcal was greater in participants with higher BMI. In addition, the PPG morphology index A_d/A_a, a second-derivative PPG marker of vascular tone and wave reflection, increased within 15 minutes of the meal and remained shifted at two hours at the temple region. This change persisted after adjustment for heart rate and is consistent with reduced wave reflection, possibly associated with vasodilation in vessels downstream of the aorta. These results support the feasibility of using a single temple-worn device to detect meals and measure the cardiac and vascular responses that follow in daily life, and identify the temple as a site for studying postprandial vascular changes.

items.title: Optimisation of GMP-compliant hollow-fiber culturing and scaled-up separation of mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles to overcome unexpected impact of bovine serum contaminants' transfer to end products
items.blurb: The clinical translation of mesenchymal stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles (MSC-EVs) requires scalable manufacturing strategies ensuring product purity, reproducibility, and compliance with Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards. However, fetal bovine serum (FBS)-derived contaminants may persist in EV preparations, compromising their characterization and clinical applicability. This study aimed to optimize MSC-EV production using hollow-fiber bioreactors while minimizing bovine protein contamination through improved culture and purification strategies. Extracellular vesicles from immortalized human adipose-derived MSCs were produced under different culture conditions, including FBS supplementation, partial replacement with Panexin, and use of chemically defined medium for high-density cultures (CDM-HD). EVs were purified using tangential flow filtration, fast protein liquid chromatography, and ultrafiltration, and characterized by nanoparticle tracking analysis, electron microscopy, Western blot, proteomics, and ELISA. Proteomic analysis revealed substantial bovine protein contamination under conventional FBS-containing conditions, with 11.4% of identified proteins exclusively assigned to bovine origin. Transitioning to CDM-HD reduced this proportion to 2.6%, markedly decreasing albumin abundance. Optimization of Panexin supplementation supported MSC expansion while reducing the necessary percentage of bovine serum. Although albumin became undetectable by Western blot, sensitive ELISA measurements revealed residual contamination and suggested unexpected protein carryover associated with chromatography column reuse. Importantly, using a new purification column yielded CDM-HD-derived EV preparations with albumin concentrations below ELISA assay's quantification limit (0.69 ng/mL). These findings highlight the importance of controlling both upstream culture conditions and downstream purification to prevent exogenous protein contamination, establishing a promising scalable manufacturing workflow for high-purity MSC-EVs suitable for further GMP-oriented development and future clinical translation.

It can be hard to ascertain why Grand Theft Auto VI is such a phenomenon from merely watching along with it. Equally devoted to the thrill of a violent crime story and a more mundane lifestyle fantasy, the appeal does not always translate to bystanders. Its soundtrack, however, is another story: a compilation of brand new material from some of the biggest pop, rap, rock and country artists on the planet – some of them combined in imaginative pileups of guest features – that can be enjoyed totally separately from the gameplay, if you so wish.

Starting from Zero, the opener by Justice – also composers of the game’s original score, released on 11 December – features the unmistakable voice of the Doobie Brothers’ Michael McDonald belting out an 80s-style pop ballad complete with a saxophone outro. But it is an unexpectedly intimate, emotional piece of work, a big-hearted odd-couple story, which is perhaps slightly more complex than at first appears.

Emma Fogarty is a smart, garrulous woman from Abbeyleix in County Laois in the Republic of Ireland who has EB: epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition which means that her skin is permanently, agonisingly painful and requires a daily calvary of bandaging and re-bandaging. items.title: From Rainfall Forecasts to Anticipatory Action: A Flood Digital Twin at Work in Dolo Ado, Ethiopia (November 2026)
items.blurb:
Country: Ethiopia
Source: CGIAR

Please refer to the attached file.

Citation

Haile, Alemseged Tamiru, Eden Seifu Gebre, Getahun Kebede Mengistie, Abel Negussie Alemu, and Hugox Retief. 2026. From Rainfall Forecasts to Anticipatory Action: A Flood Digital Twin at Work in Dolo Ado, Ethiopia. International Water Management Institute.

Abstract/Description

Flood Early Warning Bulletins translate forecasts into clear, timely, actionable information for preparedness, anticipatory action, and emergency response. By presenting expected conditions, potential impacts, and recommended actions in a standard format, they help government agencies, humanitarian organizations, and at-risk communities coordinate decisions before floods occur. Yet fragmented datasets, disconnected modelling workflows, and manual processes often delay bulletins and shorten the time available to protect lives, livelihoods, and infrastructure.

To address this gap, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), national government institutions, and development partners developed the Dolo Ado Digital Twin-based Flood Early Warning System. It creates a digital replica of the floodplain, enables two-way data exchange with communities, and integrates global databases, field surveys, and district data. HEC-HMS converts rainfall forecasts into flood forecasts, while HEC-RAS simulates likely inundation, including water depth and flood duration across the river and floodplain.

A key achievement is the co-created Flood Early Warning Bulletin, refined by stakeholders through consultations, co-design workshops, technical training, and continuous feedback. An automated workflow rapidly converts reliable Digital Twin forecasts into standardized warnings, with content, visuals, terminology, and format tailored to operational needs. The bulletin enables government agencies, humanitarian organizations, and disaster risk management authorities to make timely, coordinated decisions before and during floods.

items.title: World: ¿Cómo acompañar a sobrevivientes de violencia basada en género?
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

En contextos de conflicto y crisis, hasta el 70 % de las mujeres enfrenta algún tipo de violencia. Reconocer esta realidad, diseñar soluciones para protegerlas y apostar por formas de trabajo que no perpetúen las amenazas contra la vida y el bienestar de las mujeres es una de nuestras prioridades. En este artículo compartimos recomendaciones para ofrecer una respuesta humanitaria segura, digna y sin revictimización.

Cuando ocurre una emergencia o un desastre, las redes de apoyo institucional y comunitario se debilitan, los medios de vida se interrumpen y las desigualdades y vulnerabilidades previas se agudizan. Como resultado, en entornos afectados por crisis, hasta el 70 % de las mujeres enfrenta situaciones de violencia, casi el doble de la tasa registrada fuera de las zonas de crisis.

El desafío es aún más urgente ante las brechas globales de prevención y atención a la violencia. Solo en 2025, se reportó que el 50% de las personas sobrevivientes de violencia basada en género (VBG) no tuvo acceso a servicios esenciales como espacios seguros, atención médica, apoyo psicosocial, protección o asistencia legal, dejando al menos a un millón de mujeres y niñas sin atención vital.

Al mismo tiempo, las organizaciones de mujeres reportan un aumento en la demanda de servicios desde enero de 2025 e indican que la mayoría ya no logran cubrir los niveles actuales de necesidad en un momento marcado por recortes al financiamiento humanitario.

En los 16 Días de Activismo contra la Violencia de Género, que se extienden del 25 de noviembre, Día Internacional de la Eliminación de la Violencia contra la Mujer, al 10 de diciembre, Día de los Derechos Humanos, la Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media Luna Roja (IFRC) reafirma la prioridad de poner en el centro la protección de las sobrevivientes en cada respuesta de emergencia.

Los equipos humanitarios deben actuar bajo la premisa de que la violencia basada en género ocurre en toda crisis y deben tomar medidas de protección coherentes con las normas humanitarias, existan o no denuncias o pruebas concretas.

Reconocer todas las caras de la violencia y actuar desde lo local

Una vida libre de violencia, la igualdad de género y el reparto equitativo de las responsabilidades familiares entre hombres y mujeres son esenciales para el bienestar personal y social. Para prevenir y responder de forma efectiva, el primer paso práctico es reconocer que la violencia basada en género adopta múltiples formas, muchas veces invisibilizadas:

  • Violencia sexual y abuso sexual.
  • Violencia doméstica o intrafamiliar.
  • Violencia económica (control o privación de recursos financieros).
  • Matrimonio forzado o precoz.
  • Prostitución forzada y explotación sexual.

Dentro de los espacios de voluntariado de la Cruz Roja y la Media Luna Roja en todo el mundo, el liderazgo y la experiencia de las mujeres son indispensables para construir sistemas de protección seguros y eficaces.

La prevención comienza desde el diseño mismo de las operaciones, desde habilitar espacios seguros para mujeres, niñez y poblaciones LGBTQIA+, hasta garantizar insumos dignos para la gestión de la salud menstrual, mapear rutas de derivación segura e impulsar la representación diversa en todos los niveles de liderazgo.

5 claves para acompañar con dignidad y no hacer daño

Todas las acciones para abordar la violencia basada en género deben regirse por el principio de no hacer daño y estar centradas en la persona sobreviviente. Si una persona comparte una situación de violencia, estas cinco pautas guían una primera respuesta ética y segura:

1. Escuchar sin juzgar ni interrumpir

Para asegurar la comodidad y seguridad de la persona, es importante habilitar un espacio privado, confidencial y seguro. Escuche con atención como parte de los primeros auxilios psicológicos, sin emitir opiniones, cuestionamientos ni juicios sobre lo ocurrido. Permita que la persona exprese sus emociones libremente, sin minimizar sus sentimientos ni darle consejos no solicitados.

2. Pedir consentimiento y respetar la confidencialidad

El personal humanitario debe respetar los tiempos de la persona sobreviviente y evitar presionarla para que cuente más de lo que desea. Pedirle que repita su relato una y otra vez, o hacer interrogatorios detallados sin ser personal especializado genera revictimización. La labor humanitaria no es investigar, sino acompañar y facilitar derivaciones seguras. Además, nunca se deben compartir los datos ni derivar un caso adulto sin su consentimiento expreso e informado, salvo que exista un riesgo vital inminente.

3. Adaptar el entorno y asegurar la inclusión

Cuando acompañamos a una persona que ha sobrevivido a violencia de género debemos garantizar un trato afirmativo, accesible y libre de prejuicios, asegurando que ninguna persona esté desprotegida.

Las mujeres y niñas con discapacidad enfrentan tasas más altas de violencia y suelen contar con menos servicios adaptados. Podemos eliminar barreras físicas y comunicacionales utilizando lenguaje claro, apoyo visual o intérpretes si es necesario, e involucrpandoles activamente en el diseño de las soluciones.

También debemos evitar suposiciones sobre el género u orientación sexual de la persona, y utilizar siempre el nombre y los pronombres que la persona indique.

Asegurar la inclusión implica facilitar que la persona se involucre activamente en cada decisión sobre su proceso, ejerciendo sus derechos, deseos y la seguridad de su familia.

4. Realizar derivaciones seguras de emergencias médicas

La violencia sexual es una emergencia médica que requiere atención en las primeras 72 horas para prevenir infecciones de transmisión sexual (incluido el VIH), embarazos no deseados y secuelas físicas o psicológicas. Compartir información confiable y accesible sobre los servicios médicos, psicosociales, legales y de apoyo económico disponibles en la comunidad, es parte de la atención en salud. Esta acción no condiciona al personal de salud a presentar una denuncia, pero sí conecta a la persona con redes especializadas de forma segura y confidencial.

5. Proteger a la niñez y adolescencia

La protección de la niñez y la adolescencia es una responsabilidad compartida y exige protocolos estrictos para no exponer a la niñez y la adolescencia a mayores riesgos.

En un entorno privado y seguro, debemos asegurarnos de que la persona menor de edad sepa que vamos a creer en su palabra y que sabemos que no fue su culpa.

Si existe peligro inminente, debemos resguardar al niño, niña o adolescente lejos de la persona agresora, sin confrontarla directamente para evitar riesgos mayores y activa de inmediato las alertas ante las autoridades de protección y seguridad correspondientes.

Posteriormente debemos derivar el caso hacia los organismos oficiales de protección de la infancia y servicios especializados de salud y primeros auxilios psicológicos, evitando entrevistas profundas que puedan causar revictimización.

El personal humanitario también debe mantener acompañada e informada a la familia o red segura durante todo el proceso.

Prevención y cuidados desde el terreno

Proteger a las comunidades exige que las operaciones humanitarias sean un entorno íntegro y seguro. En la IFRC rige una política estricta de Tolerancia Cero frente a cualquier forma de acoso, discriminación, explotación o abuso sexual.

Las reglas de salvaguarda son innegociables para todo el personal y el voluntariado:

  • Cero tolerancia a cualquier actividad sexual con niños, niñas y adolescentes.
  • Está estrictamente prohibido ofrecer dinero, empleo, bienes, servicios o asistencia humanitaria a cambio de favores sexuales.
  • No se permiten relaciones sexuales entre el personal humanitario y las personas atendidas, ni el uso indebido del cargo o la jerarquía.

Cualquier sospecha de conducta indebida, explotación, abuso sexual, acoso o vulneración de la integridad puede reportarse de forma segura y confidencial a través de la línea de integridad de la IFRC en www.ifrc.integrityline.org, al correo electrónico [email protected] o llamando de manera gratuita al +41 800 437 272.

Un llamado urgente a la acción

La violencia contra las mujeres y las niñas es una violación de los derechos humanos para la que no existe excusa. Para revertir esta crisis, la red de la IFRC hace un llamado a gobiernos, donantes y organizaciones aliadas a actuar en cinco frentes prioritarios:

  • Proteger a las personas sobrevivientes.
  • Mantener los servicios esenciales y salvaguardar su financiamiento sostenido.
  • Garantizar la justicia y la rendición de cuentas para poner fin a la impunidad.
  • Fortalecer la prevención y respuesta lideradas localmente, invirtiendo en el liderazgo de las mujeres.
  • Integrar la protección en cada etapa de la acción humanitaria.

Los derechos humanos pertenecen a todas las personas; la seguridad también debe serlo. Erradicar la violencia contra las mujeres y las niñas es una tarea colectiva que empieza por creer, escuchar sin prejuicios y garantizar que cada espacio de apoyo sea verdaderamente seguro y digno.

items.title: World: How can we support survivors of gender-based violence?
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

In conflict and crisis settings, up to 70% of women face some form of violence. Recognizing this reality, designing solutions to protect them, and committing to ways of working that do not perpetuate threats to women's lives and well-being is one of our priorities. In this article, we share recommendations for delivering a safe, dignified humanitarian response that avoids revictimization.

When an emergency or disaster strikes, institutional and community support networks weaken, livelihoods are disrupted, and pre-existing inequalities and vulnerabilities deepen. As a result, in crisis-affected settings, up to 70% of women experience violence, nearly double the rate recorded outside crisis zones.

The challenge is even more urgent given global gaps in violence prevention and care. In 2025 alone, 50% of survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) were reported to lack access to essential services such as safe spaces, health care, psychosocial support, protection, or legal assistance, leaving at least one million women and girls without vital care.

At the same time, women's organizations report an increase in demand for services since January 2025 and indicate that most can no longer meet current levels of need at a time marked by humanitarian funding cuts.

During the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence, running from November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, to December 10, International Human Rights Day, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) reaffirms its priority of placing the protection of survivors at the centre of every emergency response.

Humanitarian teams must operate on the premise that gender-based violence occurs in every crisis and must take protective measures consistent with humanitarian standards, whether or not formal reports or concrete evidence exist.

Recognizing all forms of violence and acting locally

A life free from violence, gender equality, and the equitable sharing of family responsibilities between women and men are essential for personal and social well-being. To prevent and respond effectively, the first practical step is recognizing that gender-based violence takes many forms, often hidden from view:

  • Sexual violence and sexual abuse.
  • Domestic or intimate partner violence.
  • Economic violence (control or deprivation of financial resources).
  • Forced or child marriage.
  • Forced prostitution and sexual exploitation.

Within Red Cross and Red Crescent volunteering spaces worldwide, women's leadership and expertise are indispensable to building safe and effective protection systems.

Prevention begins at the very design stage of operations, from setting up safe spaces for women, children, and LGBTQIA+ populations, to ensuring dignified supplies for menstrual health management, mapping safe referral pathways, and promoting diverse representation at all levels of leadership.

5 keys to supporting survivors with dignity and doing no harm

All actions to address gender-based violence must be guided by the "do no harm" principle and remain survivor-centred. If someone discloses an experience of violence, these five guidelines steer an ethical and safe initial response:

1. Listen without judging or interrupting

To ensure the person's comfort and safety, provide a private, confidential, and safe space. Listen attentively as part of psychological first aid, without offering opinions, questioning, or judging what happened. Allow the person to express their emotions freely, without minimizing their feelings or giving unsolicited advice.

2. Ask for consent and respect confidentiality

Humanitarian personnel must respect the survivor's pace and avoid pressuring them to share more than they wish. Asking them to repeat their story over and over, or conducting detailed questioning without specialized training, causes revictimization. Humanitarian work is not about investigating, but about supporting and facilitating safe referrals. Furthermore, personal data must never be shared, nor an adult case referred, without the survivor's express and informed consent, unless there is an imminent threat to life.

3. Adapt the environment and ensure inclusion

When supporting a survivor of gender-based violence, we must guarantee affirmative, accessible, and bias-free treatment, ensuring that no one is left unprotected.

Women and girls with disabilities experience higher rates of violence and often have fewer accessible services available to them. We can remove physical and communication barriers by using clear language, visual aids, or interpreters when needed, and by actively involving them in designing solutions.

We must also avoid making assumptions about a person's gender or sexual orientation, and always use the name and pronouns they indicate.

Ensuring inclusion means enabling the person to participate actively in every decision regarding their process, upholding their rights, wishes, and the safety of their family.

4. Make safe referrals for medical emergencies

Sexual violence is a medical emergency that requires care within the first 72 hours to prevent sexually transmitted infections (including HIV), unintended pregnancies, and physical or psychological harm. Sharing reliable, accessible information about medical, psychosocial, legal, and economic support services available in the community is part of health care. This action does not obligate health personnel to file a legal report, but it connects the person with specialized networks safely and confidentially.

5. Protect children and adolescents

Protecting children and adolescents is a shared responsibility and requires strict protocols to avoid exposing them to further harm.

In a private and safe environment, we must ensure the child or adolescent knows we believe them and that what happened was not their fault.

If there is imminent danger, we must move the child or adolescent away from the perpetrator, without confronting the perpetrator directly to avoid greater risks, and immediately alert the relevant child protection and safety authorities.

Subsequently, we must refer the case to official child protection agencies and specialized health and psychological first aid services, avoiding in-depth interviews that could cause revictimization.

Humanitarian personnel must also keep the family or safe support network accompanied and informed throughout the entire process.

Prevention and care from the field

Protecting communities requires humanitarian operations to be safe environments of high integrity. The IFRC enforces a strict Zero Tolerance policy against any form of harassment, discrimination, sexual exploitation, or abuse.

Safeguarding rules are non-negotiable for all staff and volunteers:

  • Zero tolerance for any sexual activity with children and adolescents.
  • Offering money, employment, goods, services, or humanitarian assistance in exchange for sexual favours is strictly prohibited.
  • Sexual relationships between humanitarian personnel and the people they assist, as well as any misuse of position or hierarchy, are prohibited.

Any suspicion of misconduct, sexual exploitation and abuse, harassment, or integrity violations can be reported safely and confidentially through the IFRC Integrity Line at www.ifrc.integrityline.org, by email at [email protected], or by calling toll-free at +41 800 437 272.

An urgent call to action

Violence against women and girls is a human rights violation for which there is no excuse. To reverse this crisis, the IFRC network calls on governments, donors, and partner organizations to act on five priority fronts:

  • Maintain essential services and safeguard sustained funding.
  • Ensure justice and accountability to end impunity.
  • Strengthen locally led prevention and response by investing in women's leadership.
  • Integrate protection into every stage of humanitarian action.

Human rights belong to everyone; safety must too. Ending violence against women and girls is a collective effort that begins with believing, listening without prejudice, and ensuring that every space of support is truly safe and dignified.
